name: Esipher – AI Site to Theme Converter
author: Inwebtify

sections.description:
AI site builders produce a polished Vite/React + Tailwind site in minutes, exported as a ZIP. Esipher turns that export into a real, activatable theme. The core conversion – extraction, parsing, asset rewriting, theme generation and installation – runs entirely on your own server: no third-party upload service, no external API call.

Work from the admin screen (Esipher in wp-admin) or from WP-CLI (wp esipher convert).

Two optional features connect to third-party APIs, and only when you set them up (see “External services” below):

  • Esipher > Connected Projects – connect your own GitHub account and repo. GitHub rebuilds on every push and Esipher shows an “Apply update” button; an administrator clicks it to update the theme. Nothing is installed or activated without that click.
  • Esipher > Mobile App – Esipher generates a build project in a GitHub repo you own; GitHub Actions builds a native Android (and, optionally, iOS) app from your site.

This is an early development build; per-builder adapters beyond the generic fallback and a conversion history/rollback screen are still to come.

What does not convert

  • Supabase-backed auth, database reads/writes, and live data – detected and reported, never silently dropped.
  • Client-side routing beyond what exists in the built HTML.
  • Custom component layouts (cards, nav bars, icons) – these display exactly as exported, but aren’t broken into individually editable pieces yet. Headings, paragraphs, and images within multi-page conversions are: they come through as real, native Block Editor blocks.

External services

The core “upload a ZIP and get a theme” flow makes no external requests. The features below
do, and only after you enable them and provide your own credentials. You can use the plugin
indefinitely without ever touching them.

GitHub (github.com, api.github.com)

Used by Connected Projects and Mobile App. When you connect a repo, sync, or build an
app, the plugin talks to the GitHub REST API as your own GitHub account, using an OAuth access
token you obtain by authorising your own GitHub OAuth App. It sends: that access token, the
repository owner and name you enter, the contents of the build workflow file it commits into
your repo, webhook configuration (including a random shared secret), Actions repository
secrets and variables it sets for the build, and, for the Mobile App feature, an
App-Store-Connect-signed certificate request routed to Apple (see below). It downloads the
build artifacts your workflow produces. The OAuth sign-in also redirects your browser to
github.com. For Connected Projects, GitHub also calls this site’s REST route
(/wp-json/esipher/v1/github-webhook) when a build finishes; the request is verified with the
webhook’s shared secret and only records that an update is ready. Nothing is sent to GitHub
unless you have connected an account.

GitHub Terms of Service: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/github-terms/github-terms-of-service
GitHub Privacy Statement: https://docs.github.com/en/site-policy/privacy-policies/github-general-privacy-statement

Apple App Store Connect (api.appstoreconnect.apple.com)

Used by the Mobile App feature only, and only if you fill in the iOS fields (Apple Team
ID, App Store Connect API Key ID, Issuer ID and .p8 key). When you save those and start an
iOS build, the plugin calls the App Store Connect API, authenticating with a short-lived
JSON Web Token it signs locally with your .p8 key. It sends: a certificate signing request
(to obtain an Apple Distribution certificate), your app’s bundle identifier (to register it
if needed), and a request to create an App Store provisioning profile. It receives the
certificate and provisioning profile, which are stored encrypted on your site and set as
GitHub Actions secrets for the build. No request is made to Apple unless you provide an App
Store Connect API key.

Apple Media Services Terms: https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/itunes/
Apple Privacy Policy: https://www.apple.com/legal/privacy/

Original project image hosting (opt-in)

The multi-page conversion option “Try to recover cloud-hosted images from the original
project” (and the WP-CLI --recover-images flag) fetches image files from the URL your AI
site builder still hosts them at (for Lovable exports this is a *.lovableproject.com
address derived from a descriptor file inside your own export). The request sends only a normal
HTTP GET for each image path, so the host sees your site’s IP address. This happens only for that
one opt-in setting, and only for images your export references but did not bundle. No other
request is made to that host. This service is provided by Lovable.

Lovable Terms of Service: https://lovable.dev/terms
Lovable Privacy Policy: https://lovable.dev/privacy
sections.installation:
1. Upload the plugin to /wp-content/plugins/esipher, or install it from the Plugins screen.
  2. Activate it through the “Plugins” screen.
  3. Open Esipher in the wp-admin menu and upload your export ZIP, or run
    wp esipher convert from WP-CLI.
sections.faq:
Is there a video walkthrough?

Yes: https://youtu.be/6-ne9-7Wgt4 covers exporting from Lovable, building it with the Esipher Build template, and converting it here, start to finish.

Does my code ever leave my server?

No. The entire conversion pipeline – extraction, parsing, asset rewriting, theme generation, and installation – runs locally within your WordPress install.

Can Esipher skip the manual export/upload entirely and just stay in sync?

Yes, under Esipher > Connected Projects. Connect your own GitHub account (you register a free GitHub OAuth App once and paste its Client ID/Secret in – no third-party broker, same “your account, your server” model as the rest of this plugin), then connect the GitHub repo your AI builder syncs to (e.g. GitHub sync from the Lovable or Bolt.new project menu). Esipher commits a small build workflow into that repo and registers a webhook; from then on, every push builds on GitHub and Esipher flags it as “Update ready”; an administrator clicks “Apply update” to download that build and update the theme – no export, no template repo, no manual artifact download. The incoming webhook only records that a build is ready: it can never install or activate anything by itself. A “Sync now” button triggers a rebuild without waiting for your next push. This is separate from, and doesn’t replace, the manual ZIP-upload flow below.

My Lovable or Bolt.new export was rejected as “raw source, not a build” – what do I do?

Esipher converts a Vite build’s finished output, not a project’s raw, uncompiled source. If you exported straight from Lovable or Bolt.new and have never run a build on it, use the Esipher Build template: a free, one-click GitHub Actions workflow made for this. Open that page, click “Use this template” to get your own copy, upload your export’s raw .zip to it, and a build runs automatically – no installs, no command line. Download the finished result from that run’s Artifacts and upload it to Esipher instead of the original file.

This template is the recommended path for Lovable and Bolt.new exports; StackBlitz (build in your own browser) is a general-purpose fallback for other builders’ exports.
sections.changelog:
0.2.1

  • Fix: plugin author is now shown correctly in the directory.

0.2.0

  • New: Bolt.new exports are supported alongside Lovable (built Vite/React output converts the same way; raw Bolt.new source is detected and pointed at the Esipher Build template), and Connected Projects works with Bolt.new’s GitHub sync as well.
  • New: Esipher > Connected Projects – connect a GitHub-synced AI-builder repo
    once (your own OAuth App, your own account). Every push builds on GitHub; a
    webhook (with an hourly cron safety net) flags “Update ready” and an
    administrator applies it with one click. A manual “Sync now” button
    triggers a rebuild.
  • Fix: the GitHub connection now also requests the “workflow” OAuth scope,
    which GitHub requires to commit the build workflow file. Without it,
    connecting a project failed with a bare “Not Found”. If you connected a
    GitHub account on an earlier build, disconnect and reconnect once to grant
    the added permission – the settings screen warns when this is needed.
  • Fix: downloading a build artifact failed with “HTTP 401” – the request to
    the artifact’s signed storage URL was still carrying the GitHub auth
    header. The download now follows that redirect without it.
  • Fix: an auto-sync would report “Up to date” while the site still showed a
    different theme. With “Keep this theme active” enabled (the default), a
    connected project now re-activates its theme on any sync where the site
    isn’t already on it, not only the first – and a successful sync that
    leaves the theme inactive now says so instead of a bare “Up to date”.
  • Fix: disconnecting a project now always forgets it locally even if GitHub
    won’t remove the webhook, so a later reconnect starts from a clean slate
    instead of silently reusing stale sync state.
  • New: multi-page conversions now bundle a tiny dependency-free script that
    restores the mobile menu. Because a multi-page conversion ships no framework
    JavaScript, the hamburger button had nothing wiring it up; the helper wires
    it – toggling an existing hidden menu panel, or, when the panel only existed
    in the framework’s runtime, synthesising one from the nav’s own links.
  • New: Esipher > Mobile App – wrap the site in a native app. Esipher generates
    a Capacitor project in a GitHub repo you own and a bundled GitHub Actions
    workflow builds it:

    • Android (always): a debug APK (sideload to test) and a signed release AAB
      (for the Google Play Console). The signing keystore is generated in pure
      PHP (no Java), stored encrypted, and set as encrypted repo secrets.
    • iOS (optional, “iOS” tab): a signed .ipa for App Store Connect / TestFlight,
      built on a macOS runner. Needs a paid Apple Developer account and an App
      Store Connect API key (Team ID, Key ID, Issuer ID, .p8) – leave those blank
      and the iOS build is skipped. From that key Esipher provisions a
      distribution certificate and an App Store provisioning profile via the App
      Store Connect API (no Mac, no manual certificate steps), stores them
      encrypted, and the workflow signs with them.
      Android and iOS build independently: the Android tab builds Android only, the
      iOS tab builds iOS only, and an “Rebuild Android + iOS” button builds both.
      So an Apple-side problem never blocks or red-flags an Android build.
      Uses the same GitHub connection as Connected Projects.
  • Change: removed the server-side “build it now” / wp esipher convert --build
    option, which ran a project’s own npm/yarn/pnpm/bun install and build on the
    server. Build raw source with the Esipher Build GitHub template, a local
    build, or Connected Projects instead, then upload/sync the output.
  • Housekeeping: uploads now go through wp_handle_upload(); ZIP extraction and
    cleanup go through WP_Filesystem; renamed to “Esipher – AI Site to Theme
    Converter”.

0.1.0

  • Initial development build: headless conversion engine driven by WP-CLI, generic adapter only.

short_description: Convert Lovable, Bolt.new and other Vite/React site exports into a theme on your own server. Optional GitHub sync and mobile app builds.
